claim: Each subagent starts with a fresh, isolated context window; it does not see the parent's conversation history, skills already invoked, or files already read. The parent writes a delegation message; the subagent works from that.
applies_when: Deciding whether a task can be delegated cheaply: anything needing the parent's accumulated context pays to re-supply it in the prompt, and a non-fork subagent pays its own startup context.

claim: A subagent's tool work stays in its own context; the parent gets back only the summary/final result. Docs: the subagent 'does that work in its own context and returns only the summary'. Vantaige measurement: 'only the final message returns to the parent conversation'.
applies_when: Verbose, read-heavy work (search, test output, logs, doc fetches) where the parent only needs a conclusion. This is the main token-saving mechanism.

claim: Measured on one task (find a deprecated model ID across a repo): parent-only run had 52 tool calls in parent and 47,812 parent input tokens (49,452 total billed); with a research subagent the parent saw 1 Agent call and 2,104 input tokens, but total billed was 21,840 (subagent ~19,700), a 55.8% total reduction, not 95%.
applies_when: Single-author measurement on one repo-search task from session JSON files; use as an order-of-magnitude example of parent-context savings, not a benchmark. Total billed fell only ~56% because the subagent's own run is billed.

claim: Anthropic's multi-agent research system: agents typically use about 4x the tokens of chat; multi-agent systems about 15x the tokens of chat. Token usage alone explains 80% of variance in its research eval.
applies_when: Budgeting a parallel, research-style multi-agent setup with a lead agent and several subagents. Gains came from spending more tokens in parallel, so this is a cost to justify, not a saving.

claim: Anthropic reports its multi-agent system (Opus 4 lead, Sonnet 4 subagents) outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on its internal research eval; it says multi-agent 'work mainly because they help spend enough tokens to solve the problem'.
applies_when: Parallelisable breadth-first research where a single context runs out or searches sequentially. Anthropic says it fits tasks where value is high enough to pay the token cost; it says most coding tasks have fewer parallelisable pieces.

claim: Anthropic: multi-agent systems fit 'valuable tasks that involve heavy parallelization'; domains needing all agents to share the same context are a poor fit today; most coding tasks involve fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research.
applies_when: Choosing sub-agents vs one agent for coding work: tightly coupled edits with shared context should stay in the main agent.

claim: Anthropic engineering: subagents store their work in external systems and pass lightweight references back to the coordinator, which reduces token overhead from copying large outputs through conversation history.
applies_when: Designing an orchestrator for large artifacts: have sub-agents write files or store results and return a path or id, not the content.

claim: Anthropic's own guidance on when to use subagents: use them when the task produces verbose output you do not need in main context, needs tool restrictions, or is self-contained and can return a summary. Use the main conversation for frequent back-and-forth, multi-phase shared context, quick targeted changes, or when latency matters.
applies_when: The core decision rule. Subagents win on verbose self-contained work; the main conversation wins on iterative or context-sharing work.

claim: Subagent requests count toward the same usage limits as the main conversation. Docs: 'each subagent spends tokens of its own while it runs'; cost control is 'routing tasks to faster, lower-cost models like Haiku'. Running many subagents that each return detailed results can consume significant context.
applies_when: Any fan-out: the subagent run is an additional cost on top of the parent, so it is not free even when it shrinks the parent context. Set model: haiku for simple subagent work.

claim: A fork is a subagent that inherits the entire conversation so far instead of starting fresh. Docs: 'a fork costs less than a fresh subagent for tasks that need the same context'. Forks can't spawn further forks. Fork mode is on by default in interactive sessions (v2.1.232+) and off in -p and the Agent SDK.
applies_when: Work that needs the parent's context (already-read files, decisions made). A fork reuses the parent's cache prefix, so it avoids re-supplying context; a fresh subagent is cheaper only when the parent context is large and irrelevant.

claim: Subagents do not reuse the parent's prompt cache at first request: their system prompt and tool set differ, so the prefix differs. A subagent warms its own cache across its turns, and the parent's cache is unaffected by the subagent's call and result. A fork, by contrast, inherits system prompt, tools and history exactly and reads the parent cache.
applies_when: Cost model for fresh subagents: each spawn pays a full cache write of its own startup prompt. Fork is the only type that reuses the parent cache.

claim: Subagent requests fall outside the main-conversation cache TTL bucket: they get a 5-minute cache by default even on a Claude subscription (main conversation gets 1 hour there). Configure with subagentPromptCacheTtl or CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL, or a subagent's experimental cacheTtl frontmatter (v2.1.248+).
applies_when: Subagent spawns separated by more than 5 minutes pay a fresh cache write each time. Set the subagent TTL when a sub-agent is spawned repeatedly in a long session. The number is the 5-minute TTL in seconds.

claim: Agent-team and subagent cost guidance from Anthropic docs: agent teams use approximately 7x more tokens than standard sessions when teammates run in plan mode; token cost scales with team size; use Sonnet for teammates and shut them down when done. Subagents: 'Lower: results summarized back to main context' vs teams 'Higher: each teammate is a separate Claude instance'.
applies_when: Choosing between subagents and agent teams: teams need peer messaging and cost several times a single session; subagents report back and are cheaper. Use teams only for research, review or parallel debugging where teammates must challenge each other.

claim: Subagent nesting: by default a subagent can spawn subagents up to three layers below the main conversation; CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH sets the limit (1 turns nesting off). The vantaige article's claim that subagents cannot spawn subagents is out of date.
applies_when: Designing multi-level orchestration: a depth of 3 multiplies spawn costs. Set the depth env var to 1 or 2 to cap a fan-out tree.

claim: Cold-start cost of a fresh subagent measured from local transcripts (~1,777 subagents, 95 sessions, one developer): a cold-start subagent context is about 37k tokens, of which about 950 (~3%) is the unique task; about 80% is rewritten from scratch on each spawn and about 16% is served from cache. Reads 0.1x, 5-minute writes 1.25x, 1-hour writes 2.0x.
applies_when: Estimating the fixed overhead per spawn for a fresh subagent with a large system prompt and tool set. The per-spawn overhead is the reason tiny tasks lose. This is a mirror of anthropics/claude-code issue 74318, not an Anthropic statement.

claim: Same mirror of anthropics/claude-code issue 74318 (open, opened 2026-07-05): modeled ~14.3% saving on subagent prompt spend ($2,768 to $2,373) and ~7.8% of overall spend; a subagent hits the shared prefix 85% of the time when a same-type sibling ran within 5 minutes, and 45% when none did. Parent caches expired while blocked on a child in 96% of measured cases (median idle gap ~9 min).
applies_when: Long-running parents that wait on a sub-agent: the parent's cache can expire during the wait, so the parent pays a rewrite on resume. Savings are modeled, not billed; check the GitHub issue for status.

claim: Claimed (not confirmed) that subagents read the parent's cache: a reporter saw subagents with ~154k and ~159k cache_read_input_tokens from ~2K-token prompts in a 150K-token parent session; the issue reports dispatch success falling from ~100% to ~33% in the long session. Issue closed as not planned on 2026-08-08.
applies_when: Only as a warning about long parents: if the claim holds, a Agent dispatch in a very long session carries parent context. Anthropic's own prompt-caching doc says subagents start with their own prefix, which contradicts this claim, so treat it as unresolved.
